title: HS2 development around Euston could support 6,000 new homes
content: More than 6,000 new homes could be built around Euston as part of the HS2 development, with proposals spanning railway land, housing estates, and redevelopment sites from Bloomsbury to Camley Street. Euston housing zones (c) MHCLG A high-level brochure produced by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) sets out, in broad terms, a 30-plus-year plan to build new housing and neighbourhoods around Euston station. The plan extends beyond the redevelopment of Euston station itself, identifying six surrounding zones where additional housing could be built. One of the earliest projects would be at Regent’s Park Estate North, where council-led proposals could deliver around 500 new homes. The brochure presents this as a starting point for wider investment and potential renewal across the estate. A substantial opportunity also lies at Euston station and its railway cuttings, with housing potentially built above and alongside the tracks, as well as on land associated with HS2. Sites identified include the former Royal Mail site, Maria Fidelis and Starcross Street. The brochure argues that these should be considered together to make the most of the available land, rather than developed as isolated plots. The report also suggests that reconfiguring railway infrastructure, consolidating servicing facilities, and improving access could free up more space for development, allowing new homes to be built in phases alongside the transport works. Across the existing Regent’s Park Estate, the proposals envisage a longer-term estate renewal programme and additional housing, developed with existing residents. Addressing overcrowding is one reason for exploring new homes in and around the estate. The nearby Barracks site is also mentioned as a possible development opportunity, although only if its operational requirements change. It is currently expected to remain in use. South of the station, Euston Road and Bloomsbury could accommodate housing through redevelopment along the main road and the potential conversion or replacement of some institutional buildings. Within Bloomsbury, the brochure suggests repurposing some educational or institutional buildings for housing where they are less suitable for their current use. This would depend on providing replacement educational space and respecting the area’s established character. To the east and north-east of the station, Somers Town and Mornington Crescent offer further opportunities through estate renewal. The sixth area is Camley Street, where a first phase of regeneration already has planning consent for a mixed-use neighbourhood containing new homes, affordable housing and employment space. The brochure calls for housing and neighbourhood renewal to become central objectives of the Euston programme. It also acknowledges that surrounding communities have endured prolonged disruption while seeing limited benefits so far. Although the report expects there to be a significant proportion of affordable and social rented housing, it does not set an overall percentage or outline any planning designs for the new estates. At this stage, it’s more about setting out very broad aspirations while leaving the dirty details to later. The next step is a Strategic Delivery Framework, due to be developed during 2026–27, which would examine infrastructure, funding, viability and the order in which sites could come forward. The proposed timetable also points towards establishing a Locally Led Urban Development Corporation for Euston in 2027. If that deadline is met, then some of the new houses might even be built in time for Euston station’s bicentenary in 2037. The brochure is here.
